source_text:
εἴπερ δὲ καὶ σὺ

σωφρονεῖν θέλῃς, φίλος, μὴ τὴν πάρεργον τῆς γραφῆς σκόπει θέαν, τὴν τοῦ λόγου
δὲ πρῶτα συνδρομὴν μάθε· νυμφοστολεῖ γὰρ τοὺς ποθοῦντας ἐμφρόνως.
thought_title: The reader's task: attend to the story's movement, not the writing's spectacle
orientation: The author is addressing the reader directly, urging him to look past the incidental spectacle of the writing and learn the story's movement first, because the work escorts wise lovers to the bridal chamber.
pass_a_gloss: But if you also wish to live chastely, friend, do not look at the incidental spectacle of the writing, but first learn the movement of the story; for it escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'live chastely' for σωφρονεῖν, preserving the infinitive's force as the content of the wish.

choices.english: the incidental spectacle of the writing
choices.why: πάρεργον means 'incidental' or 'secondary,' and θέα means 'spectacle' or 'sight'; the phrase contrasts with the story's movement, so 'incidental spectacle' captures the sense of a by-product of the writing.
rejected: the secondary sight of the writing
the incidental view of the writing

choices.why: The glossary requires 'movement' for συνδρομή, referring to the plot's development or flow, which the reader should attend to first.
The glossary requires 'escorts to the bridal chamber' for νυμφοστολεῖ, preserving the metaphorical sense of leading wise lovers to union.
ποθοῦντας is the present participle of ποθέω, 'to long for, love'; rendering it as 'those who love' keeps the participial force and the erotic sense without over-translating.
The glossary requires 'wisely' for ἐμφρόνως, modifying the lovers' manner of being escorted.

pass_b_english: And if you too, my friend, wish to live chastely, do not dwell on the incidental spectacle of the writing; learn first the movement of the story. For it escorts those who love wisely to the bridal chamber.

problems.why: Same Greek term rendered as 'story' and 'movement of the story'
Adjective 'chaste' vs adverb 'chastely' may obscure same Greek root
problems.fix: Note consistent Greek sophrosyne underlying all

problems.quote: attend first to the movement of the story
problems.why: The key imperative verb shifts from 'attend' to 'learn' between the main text and the remnant, changing the reader's prescribed action.
problems.fix: Use the same verb in both; 'attend' better conveys the Greek sense of paying attention to narrative movement.

variants.text: attend first to the movement of the story
learn first the movement of the story

edits.old: learn first the movement of the story
edits.new: attend first to the movement of the story

fixed: The glossary concern about 'story' vs 'movement of the story' is not a translation error: the source uses λόγος for 'story' and συνδρομήν for 'movement', so the English correctly distinguishes them.

The glossary concern about 'chaste' vs 'chastely' is not a translation error: the source uses σώφρονα/σωφρονέστατος as adjectives and σωφρονεῖν as a verb, so the English correctly reflects the different grammatical forms.
The verb shift from 'attend' to 'learn' is a real inconsistency: the source uses the same imperative μάθε in both the main text and the remnant, so the English now uses 'attend' in both places.
